title: NY S06953: Relates to the training and use of artificial intelligence frontier models; defines terms; establishes remedies for violations.

obligations: Before deploying a frontier model, a large developer must implement a written safety and security protocol (Sec. 1421(1)(a)).

A large developer must retain an unredacted copy of the safety and security protocol, including records and dates of updates or revisions, for as long as the frontier model is deployed plus five years (Sec. 1421(1)(b)).
A large developer must conspicuously publish a copy of the safety and security protocol with appropriate redactions and transmit a copy to the attorney general (Sec. 1421(1)(c)(i)).
A large developer must grant the attorney general access to the unredacted safety and security protocol upon request (Sec. 1421(1)(c)(ii)).

A large developer must record and retain for as long as the frontier model is deployed plus five years information on specific tests and test results used in any assessment of the frontier model that provides sufficient detail for third parties to replicate the testing procedure (Sec. 1421(1)(d)).
A large developer must implement appropriate safeguards to prevent unreasonable risk of critical harm (Sec. 1421(1)(e)).

A large developer must conduct an annual review of any safety and security protocol to account for changes to capabilities and industry best practices and, if necessary, make modifications and publish the modified protocol in the same manner (Sec. 1421(3)).
A large developer must annually retain a third party to perform an independent audit of compliance with the requirements of section 1421 (Sec. 1421(4)(a)).
The third party auditor must be granted access to unredacted materials as necessary (Sec. 1421(4)(b)).

The third party must produce a report including a detailed assessment of compliance, identified instances of noncompliance and recommendations, a detailed assessment of internal controls, and the lead auditor's signature certifying results (Sec. 1421(4)(c)).
A large developer must retain an unredacted copy of the third party report for as long as the frontier model is deployed plus five years (Sec. 1421(4)(d)).
A large developer must conspicuously publish a copy of the third party report with appropriate redactions and transmit a copy to the attorney general (Sec. 1421(4)(e)(i)).
A large developer must grant the attorney general access to the unredacted third party report upon request (Sec. 1421(4)(e)(ii)).
A large developer must submit to the attorney general the updated total compute cost used to train their frontier models simultaneously with their annual third party audit report (Sec. 1421(5)).

A large developer must disclose each safety incident affecting the frontier model to the attorney general within seventy two hours of learning of the safety incident or learning facts sufficient to establish a reasonable belief that a safety incident has occurred, including the date, reasons it qualifies, and a short plain statement (Sec. 1421(6)).

A person who is not a large developer but who sets out to train a frontier model that if completed as planned would qualify such person as a large developer must, before training such model, implement a written safety and security protocol excluding the requirements described in paragraphs (c) and (d) of subdivision twelve of section 1420, and conspicuously publish a copy with appropriate redactions and transmit a copy to the attorney general (Sec. 1421(9)).

A large developer must inform employees of their protections, rights and obligations under this article by posting a notice conspicuously in easily accessible and well lighted places customarily frequented by employees (Sec. 1422(3)).
prohibitions: A large developer shall not deploy a frontier model if doing so would create an unreasonable risk of critical harm (Sec. 1421(2)).
A large developer shall not knowingly make false or materially misleading statements or omissions in or regarding documents produced pursuant to section 1421 (Sec. 1421(8)).

A large developer or a contractor or subcontractor of a large developer shall not prevent an employee from disclosing or threatening to disclose information to the large developer or the attorney general if the employee has reasonable cause to believe that the large developer's activities pose an unreasonable or substantial risk of critical harm, and shall not retaliate against an employee for such disclosure or threat (Sec. 1422(1)).

A provision within a contract or agreement that seeks to waive, preclude, or burden the enforcement of a liability arising from a violation of this article, or to shift that liability to any person or entity in exchange for their use or access of a large developer's products or services, is void as a matter of public policy (Sec. 1423(2)(a)).

It protects employees who disclose risks and authorizes the attorney general to seek civil penalties and injunctive relief.

key_definitions: Appropriate redactions: redactions to a safety and security protocol or audit report that are reasonably necessary to protect public safety or United States national security, trade secrets, or confidential information pursuant to state and federal law (Sec. 1420(1)).

Artificial intelligence: a machine based system that can, for a given set of human defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments, and that uses machine and human based inputs to perceive real and virtual environments, abstract such perceptions into models through analysis in an automated manner, and use model inference to formulate options for information or action (Sec. 1420(2)).

Artificial intelligence model: an information system or component of an information system that implements artificial intelligence technology and uses computational, statistical, or machine learning techniques to produce outputs from a given set of inputs (Sec. 1420(3)).

Compute cost: the cost incurred to pay for compute used in training a model when calculated using the average market prices of cloud compute in the United States at the start of training such model as reasonably assessed by the person doing the training (Sec. 1420(4)).

Deploy: to use a frontier model or to make a frontier model foreseeably available to one or more third parties for use, modification, copying, or a combination thereof with other software, except as reasonably necessary for training or developing the frontier model, evaluating the frontier model or other frontier models, or complying with federal or state laws (Sec. 1420(5)).

Frontier model: either an artificial intelligence model trained using greater than 10 to the 26th power computational operations, the compute cost of which exceeds one hundred million dollars, or an artificial intelligence model produced by applying knowledge distillation to such a frontier model (Sec. 1420(6)).

Critical harm: the death or serious injury of one hundred or more people or at least one billion dollars of damages to rights in money or property caused or materially enabled by a large developer's creation, use, storage, or release of a frontier model, through either the creation or use of a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapon, or an artificial intelligence model engaging in conduct that acts with limited human intervention and would, if committed by a human, constitute a crime specified in the penal law that requires intent, recklessness, or gross negligence, or the solicitation or aiding and abetting of such a crime; a harm inflicted by an intervening human actor shall not be deemed to result from a developer's activities unless such activities made it substantially easier or more likely for the actor to inflict such harm (Sec. 1420(7)).

Knowledge distillation: any supervised learning technique that uses a larger artificial intelligence model or the output of a larger artificial intelligence model to train a smaller artificial intelligence model with similar or equivalent capabilities as the larger artificial intelligence model (Sec. 1420(8)).

Large developer: a person that has trained at least one frontier model, the compute cost of which exceeds five million dollars, and has spent over one hundred million dollars in compute costs in aggregate in training frontier models; accredited colleges and universities shall not be considered large developers to the extent that such colleges and universities are engaging in academic research; if a person subsequently transfers full intellectual property rights of the frontier model to another person and retains none of those rights, then the receiving person shall be considered the large developer (Sec. 1420(9)).
Model weight: a numerical parameter in an artificial intelligence model that is adjusted through training and that helps determine how inputs are transformed into outputs (Sec. 1420(10)).

Person: an individual, proprietorship, firm, partnership, joint venture, syndicate, business trust, company, corporation, limited liability company, association, committee, or any other nongovernmental organization or group of persons acting in concert (Sec. 1420(11)).

Safety and security protocol: documented technical and organizational protocols that specify reasonable protections and procedures to reduce risk of critical harm, describe cybersecurity protections, describe testing procedure to evaluate unreasonable risk of critical harm, describe how testing assesses misuse or modification, state compliance requirements with sufficient detail, describe how the large developer will fulfill obligations, and designate senior personnel responsible for compliance (Sec. 1420(12)).

Safety incident: an incident of the following kinds that occurs in such a way that it provides demonstrable evidence of an increased risk of critical harm: a frontier model autonomously engaging in behavior other than at the request of a user; theft, misappropriation, malicious use, inadvertent release, unauthorized access, or escape of model weights; critical failure of technical or administrative controls; or unauthorized use of a frontier model (Sec. 1420(13)).

Trade secret: any form and type of financial, business, scientific, technical, economic, or engineering information that derives independent economic value from not being generally known and is subject to reasonable efforts to maintain secrecy (Sec. 1420(14)).

What it does

The RAISE act requires large developers of frontier artificial intelligence models to implement safety and security protocols, publish redacted versions, conduct annual third party audits, report safety incidents and compute costs to the attorney general, and avoid deploying models that create unreasonable risk of critical harm. It protects employees who disclose risks and authorizes the attorney general to seek civil penalties and injunctive relief.

Who it applies to

  • Large developers as defined in Sec. 1420(9)
  • Persons who are not large developers but plan to train a frontier model that would qualify them as a large developer (Sec. 1421(9))
  • Contractors and subcontractors of large developers with respect to employee protections (Sec. 1422(1))
  • Employees of large developers and their contractors or subcontractors for protections (Sec. 1422(5)(a))

Effective date

The ninetieth day after it shall have become a law (Sec. 3).

Key definitions

  • Appropriate redactions: redactions to a safety and security protocol or audit report that are reasonably necessary to protect public safety or United States national security, trade secrets, or confidential information pursuant to state and federal law (Sec. 1420(1)).
  • Artificial intelligence: a machine based system that can, for a given set of human defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments, and that uses machine and human based inputs to perceive real and virtual environments, abstract such perceptions into models through analysis in an automated manner, and use model inference to formulate options for information or action (Sec. 1420(2)).
  • Artificial intelligence model: an information system or component of an information system that implements artificial intelligence technology and uses computational, statistical, or machine learning techniques to produce outputs from a given set of inputs (Sec. 1420(3)).
  • Compute cost: the cost incurred to pay for compute used in training a model when calculated using the average market prices of cloud compute in the United States at the start of training such model as reasonably assessed by the person doing the training (Sec. 1420(4)).
  • Deploy: to use a frontier model or to make a frontier model foreseeably available to one or more third parties for use, modification, copying, or a combination thereof with other software, except as reasonably necessary for training or developing the frontier model, evaluating the frontier model or other frontier models, or complying with federal or state laws (Sec. 1420(5)).
  • Frontier model: either an artificial intelligence model trained using greater than 10 to the 26th power computational operations, the compute cost of which exceeds one hundred million dollars, or an artificial intelligence model produced by applying knowledge distillation to such a frontier model (Sec. 1420(6)).
  • Critical harm: the death or serious injury of one hundred or more people or at least one billion dollars of damages to rights in money or property caused or materially enabled by a large developer's creation, use, storage, or release of a frontier model, through either the creation or use of a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapon, or an artificial intelligence model engaging in conduct that acts with limited human intervention and would, if committed by a human, constitute a crime specified in the penal law that requires intent, recklessness, or gross negligence, or the solicitation or aiding and abetting of such a crime; a harm inflicted by an intervening human actor shall not be deemed to result from a developer's activities unless such activities made it substantially easier or more likely for the actor to inflict such harm (Sec. 1420(7)).
  • Knowledge distillation: any supervised learning technique that uses a larger artificial intelligence model or the output of a larger artificial intelligence model to train a smaller artificial intelligence model with similar or equivalent capabilities as the larger artificial intelligence model (Sec. 1420(8)).
  • Large developer: a person that has trained at least one frontier model, the compute cost of which exceeds five million dollars, and has spent over one hundred million dollars in compute costs in aggregate in training frontier models; accredited colleges and universities shall not be considered large developers to the extent that such colleges and universities are engaging in academic research; if a person subsequently transfers full intellectual property rights of the frontier model to another person and retains none of those rights, then the receiving person shall be considered the large developer (Sec. 1420(9)).
  • Model weight: a numerical parameter in an artificial intelligence model that is adjusted through training and that helps determine how inputs are transformed into outputs (Sec. 1420(10)).
  • Person: an individual, proprietorship, firm, partnership, joint venture, syndicate, business trust, company, corporation, limited liability company, association, committee, or any other nongovernmental organization or group of persons acting in concert (Sec. 1420(11)).
  • Safety and security protocol: documented technical and organizational protocols that specify reasonable protections and procedures to reduce risk of critical harm, describe cybersecurity protections, describe testing procedure to evaluate unreasonable risk of critical harm, describe how testing assesses misuse or modification, state compliance requirements with sufficient detail, describe how the large developer will fulfill obligations, and designate senior personnel responsible for compliance (Sec. 1420(12)).
  • Safety incident: an incident of the following kinds that occurs in such a way that it provides demonstrable evidence of an increased risk of critical harm: a frontier model autonomously engaging in behavior other than at the request of a user; theft, misappropriation, malicious use, inadvertent release, unauthorized access, or escape of model weights; critical failure of technical or administrative controls; or unauthorized use of a frontier model (Sec. 1420(13)).
  • Trade secret: any form and type of financial, business, scientific, technical, economic, or engineering information that derives independent economic value from not being generally known and is subject to reasonable efforts to maintain secrecy (Sec. 1420(14)).

Obligations

  • Before deploying a frontier model, a large developer must implement a written safety and security protocol (Sec. 1421(1)(a)).
  • A large developer must retain an unredacted copy of the safety and security protocol, including records and dates of updates or revisions, for as long as the frontier model is deployed plus five years (Sec. 1421(1)(b)).
  • A large developer must conspicuously publish a copy of the safety and security protocol with appropriate redactions and transmit a copy to the attorney general (Sec. 1421(1)(c)(i)).
  • A large developer must grant the attorney general access to the unredacted safety and security protocol upon request (Sec. 1421(1)(c)(ii)).
  • A large developer must record and retain for as long as the frontier model is deployed plus five years information on specific tests and test results used in any assessment of the frontier model that provides sufficient detail for third parties to replicate the testing procedure (Sec. 1421(1)(d)).
  • A large developer must implement appropriate safeguards to prevent unreasonable risk of critical harm (Sec. 1421(1)(e)).
  • A large developer must conduct an annual review of any safety and security protocol to account for changes to capabilities and industry best practices and, if necessary, make modifications and publish the modified protocol in the same manner (Sec. 1421(3)).
  • A large developer must annually retain a third party to perform an independent audit of compliance with the requirements of section 1421 (Sec. 1421(4)(a)).
  • The third party auditor must be granted access to unredacted materials as necessary (Sec. 1421(4)(b)).
  • The third party must produce a report including a detailed assessment of compliance, identified instances of noncompliance and recommendations, a detailed assessment of internal controls, and the lead auditor's signature certifying results (Sec. 1421(4)(c)).
  • A large developer must retain an unredacted copy of the third party report for as long as the frontier model is deployed plus five years (Sec. 1421(4)(d)).
  • A large developer must conspicuously publish a copy of the third party report with appropriate redactions and transmit a copy to the attorney general (Sec. 1421(4)(e)(i)).
  • A large developer must grant the attorney general access to the unredacted third party report upon request (Sec. 1421(4)(e)(ii)).
  • A large developer must submit to the attorney general the updated total compute cost used to train their frontier models simultaneously with their annual third party audit report (Sec. 1421(5)).
  • A large developer must disclose each safety incident affecting the frontier model to the attorney general within seventy two hours of learning of the safety incident or learning facts sufficient to establish a reasonable belief that a safety incident has occurred, including the date, reasons it qualifies, and a short plain statement (Sec. 1421(6)).
  • A person who is not a large developer but who sets out to train a frontier model that if completed as planned would qualify such person as a large developer must, before training such model, implement a written safety and security protocol excluding the requirements described in paragraphs (c) and (d) of subdivision twelve of section 1420, and conspicuously publish a copy with appropriate redactions and transmit a copy to the attorney general (Sec. 1421(9)).
  • A large developer must inform employees of their protections, rights and obligations under this article by posting a notice conspicuously in easily accessible and well lighted places customarily frequented by employees (Sec. 1422(3)).

Prohibitions

  • A large developer shall not deploy a frontier model if doing so would create an unreasonable risk of critical harm (Sec. 1421(2)).
  • A large developer shall not knowingly make false or materially misleading statements or omissions in or regarding documents produced pursuant to section 1421 (Sec. 1421(8)).
  • A large developer or a contractor or subcontractor of a large developer shall not prevent an employee from disclosing or threatening to disclose information to the large developer or the attorney general if the employee has reasonable cause to believe that the large developer's activities pose an unreasonable or substantial risk of critical harm, and shall not retaliate against an employee for such disclosure or threat (Sec. 1422(1)).
  • A provision within a contract or agreement that seeks to waive, preclude, or burden the enforcement of a liability arising from a violation of this article, or to shift that liability to any person or entity in exchange for their use or access of a large developer's products or services, is void as a matter of public policy (Sec. 1423(2)(a)).

Penalties and enforcement

The attorney general may bring a civil action for a violation of this article and recover civil penalties: for a violation of section 1421, a civil penalty not exceeding five percent of the total compute cost used to train the large developer's frontier models for a first violation and not exceeding fifteen percent for any subsequent violation; for a violation of section 1422, a civil penalty not exceeding ten thousand dollars per employee for each violation awarded to the employee who was retaliated against; and injunctive or declaratory relief for violations of sections 1421 or 1422 (Sec. 1423(1)). A provision in a contract that waives, precludes, or burdens enforcement of liability or shifts liability is void (Sec. 1423(2)(a)). A court may disregard corporate formalities and impose joint and several liability on affiliated entities under specified conditions (Sec. 1423(2)(b)). An employee harmed by a violation of section 1422 may petition a court for appropriate temporary or preliminary injunctive relief (Sec. 1422(2)). This section does not limit the application of other laws (Sec. 1423(3)).

How it affects AI deployment

  • An organisation that qualifies as a large developer must implement and publish a safety and security protocol before deploying any frontier model, and must retain records and grant the attorney general access to unredacted versions (Sec. 1421(1)).
  • A large developer cannot deploy a frontier model if doing so would create an unreasonable risk of critical harm, which may require pre deployment risk assessment and safeguards (Sec. 1421(1)(e) and 1421(2)).
  • A large developer must undergo an annual third party audit and publish a redacted report, which creates ongoing compliance and transparency obligations (Sec. 1421(4)).
  • A large developer must report safety incidents to the attorney general within seventy two hours, requiring incident response procedures (Sec. 1421(6)).
  • A large developer must submit updated total compute cost annually, which may expose financial information (Sec. 1421(5)).
  • A person planning to train a frontier model that would qualify them as a large developer must implement and publish a safety and security protocol before training begins (Sec. 1421(9)).
  • Violations can result in civil penalties based on a percentage of total compute cost, which could be substantial for large models, and injunctive relief (Sec. 1423(1)).
  • Contract provisions that waive or shift liability are void, and courts may impose joint and several liability on affiliated entities, increasing legal exposure (Sec. 1423(2)).
  • Large developers must post employee notices and cannot retaliate against employees who disclose risks, requiring internal whistleblower protections (Sec. 1422(1) and 1422(3)).

Notable exemptions

  • Accredited colleges and universities are not considered large developers to the extent they are engaging in academic research (Sec. 1420(9)).
  • Section 1421 does not apply to products or services to the extent that the requirements would strictly conflict with the terms of a contract with a federal government entity (Sec. 1421(7)(a)).
  • Section 1421 applies to development or deployment of a frontier model for any use that is not the subject of a contract with a federal government entity, even if the model has already been developed, trained, or used by a federal government entity (Sec. 1421(7)(b)).
  • This article shall not apply to the extent that it is preempted by federal law (Sec. 1425).

Compliance steps

  • Determine whether the organisation qualifies as a large developer under Sec. 1420(9) or plans to train a frontier model that would qualify under Sec. 1421(9).
  • Before deploying a frontier model, implement a written safety and security protocol that meets the requirements of Sec. 1420(12) (Sec. 1421(1)(a)).
  • Retain an unredacted copy of the safety and security protocol and records of updates for as long as the model is deployed plus five years (Sec. 1421(1)(b)).
  • Publish a redacted copy of the safety and security protocol and transmit it to the attorney general (Sec. 1421(1)(c)(i)).
  • Grant the attorney general access to the unredacted safety and security protocol upon request (Sec. 1421(1)(c)(ii)).
  • Record and retain test information sufficient for third parties to replicate testing procedures (Sec. 1421(1)(d)).
  • Implement safeguards to prevent unreasonable risk of critical harm (Sec. 1421(1)(e)).
  • Assess whether deployment would create an unreasonable risk of critical harm and refrain from deploying if so (Sec. 1421(2)).
  • Conduct an annual review of the safety and security protocol and publish any modifications (Sec. 1421(3)).
  • Annually retain a third party to perform an independent audit of compliance (Sec. 1421(4)(a)).
  • Grant the third party auditor access to unredacted materials (Sec. 1421(4)(b)).
  • Obtain and retain an unredacted copy of the third party audit report for as long as the model is deployed plus five years (Sec. 1421(4)(d)).
  • Publish a redacted copy of the third party report and transmit it to the attorney general (Sec. 1421(4)(e)(i)).
  • Grant the attorney general access to the unredacted third party report upon request (Sec. 1421(4)(e)(ii)).
  • Submit updated total compute cost to the attorney general simultaneously with the annual audit report (Sec. 1421(5)).
  • Establish procedures to disclose safety incidents to the attorney general within seventy two hours (Sec. 1421(6)).
  • Avoid making false or materially misleading statements or omissions in documents produced under section 1421 (Sec. 1421(8)).
  • Post a notice informing employees of their protections, rights and obligations under the article (Sec. 1422(3)).
  • Do not prevent or retaliate against employees for disclosing risks (Sec. 1422(1)).
  • If not yet a large developer but planning to train a frontier model that would qualify, implement a written safety and security protocol excluding certain testing description requirements and publish and transmit it before training (Sec. 1421(9)).

 29 of the following:

 44 intelligence model with similar or equivalent capabilities as the larger 
 45 artificial intelligence model.

 51 (a) Derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not

 53 means by, other persons who can obtain economic value from its disclo- 
 54 sure or use; and

 2 and use. 1. Before deploying a frontier model, the large developer of

 6 including records and dates of any updates or revisions. Such unredacted 
 7 copy of the safety and security protocol, including records and dates of 
 8 any updates or revisions, shall be retained for as long as the frontier 
 9 model is deployed plus five years; 
 10 (c) (i) Conspicuously publish a copy of the safety and security proto- 
 11 col with appropriate redactions and transmit a copy of such redacted 
 12 safety and security protocol to the attorney general; 
 13 (ii) Grant the attorney general access to the unredacted safety and 
 14 security protocol upon request;

 17 specific tests and test results used in any assessment of the frontier

 42 § 1422. Protections, rights and obligations of employees. 1. A large
